newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan team to discuss economic package with IMF.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan team to discuss economic package with IMF.

text.p: Senior Pakistani economic officials will head for Washington next week to discuss an emergency economic package with the International Monetary Fund, a source close to the government said on Friday.

The source said two of Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto's top economic advisers, V.A. Jafarey and Shahid Hassan Khan, would lead a team to Washington on Sunday to brief the IMF on what the government has called "bold and difficult" decisions.
"The government is working on some modifications to the IMF-proposed package and wants to discuss these first with the fund before announcing anything in Pakistan," the source said.

The government said on Thursday it had approved a framework deal drawn up with the IMF in Washington earlier this month, but gave no details of the measures, designed to reduce Pakistan's yawning current account and budget deficits.
The IMF has held up disbursements of a $600 million standby loan because of doubts about Pakistan's implementation of agreed reforms and confusion over the 1996/97 (July-June) budget.
It cannot disburse the delayed payments until a mission has visited Pakistan and completed a review of the economy.
Sources in the Finance Ministry say the IMF has made clear that it will not send a team to Islamabad until the government had come up with a credible and comprehensive package.
Bhutto's government is blaming Pakistan's economic plight on a series of strikes and opposition protests that followed the announcement of what was billed as a tough budget in June.

"The cabinet felt that in order to offset the negative impact of those strikes and other negative factors, bold and difficult decisions needed to be taken in the interest of consolidating a sustained economic growth and quickening the country's march towards meaningful progress," a government statement said after a cabinet meeting on Thursday.
"The cabinet felt that even difficult decisions will have to be so taken as to make them as painless as possible and without jeopardising in any way Pakistan's security interests."

The reference to security interests suggested that the armed forces, which soak up a big share of the budget, would not be asked for spending cuts. Defence spending is widely seen as sacrosanct because of Pakistan's bitter conflict with India.
The IMF has previously asked Pakistan to reduce its budget deficit to four percent of gross domestic product from anywhere between five and six percent in fiscal 1995/96.
IMF concern has focused on Pakistan's large current account deficit and shrinking foreign reserves, now at about $900 million, excluding gold.
Satisfying the IMF, however, could pose an acute political challenge to Bhutto's three-year-old government, already under opposition fire for alleged corruption and mismanagement.
